passages.t: Thanks to the judge who does not forget the afflicted
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. To the tune of ‘The Death of the Son.’ A Psalm of David” (verse 1).

The psalm opens with whole-hearted thanks: “I will give thanks to the LORD with all my heart; I will recount all Your wonders” (verse 1).

It tells how God has acted against the man's enemies and against whole nations. “For You have upheld my just cause; You sit on Your throne judging righteously” (verse 4).

Then comes the centre of the psalm. “But the LORD abides forever; He has established His throne for judgment” (verse 7). “He judges the world with justice; He governs the people with equity” (verse 8). “The LORD is a refuge for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble” (verse 9).

The psalm calls everyone to sing, and gives the reason: “For the Avenger of bloodshed remembers; He does not ignore the cry of the afflicted” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
‘The Death of the Son’ seems to be the name of a tune. No one knows what it refers to. Some old guesses linked it with Goliath or with one of David's sons, but those are only guesses.

Psalms 9 and 10 belong together. In Hebrew they form one acrostic, a poem where the lines begin with the letters of the alphabet in order. The pattern runs across both psalms, but it is broken: some letters are missing and some are out of place. Psalm 10 also has no heading, which is rare in this part of the book. The Greek Old Testament and the Latin Bible treat the two as one psalm. That is where the numbering of the Psalms in Greek and Latin Bibles first falls one behind the Hebrew. The book page on the Psalms explains this. Scholars debate whether the broken alphabet was damaged in copying, or whether the poet let it falter on purpose where the complaint grows.

The picture is of a king on his throne hearing cases. In Israel the king's first duty was to defend the weak. God is the king who truly does it.

‘Equity’ means fairness: the same justice for rich and poor.

‘Those who know Your name’ (verse 10) are people who know who God is and trust him. ‘Name’ means character.

‘The Avenger of bloodshed’ (verse 12) recalls a figure in Israel's law. When someone was killed, a relative called the avenger of blood had the duty to pursue justice for him (Numbers 35:19). God is that relative for the afflicted. He ‘remembers’: he keeps their cause in mind.
passages.later:
Paul, speaking in Athens, uses the words of verse 8: God “has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed” (Acts 17:31).

Hannah's song, at the start of Israel's kingdom, sings of the same God: “He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap” (1 Samuel 2:8). Mary sings it again: “He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble” (Luke 1:52).

Lamentations is also built on the alphabet, in its first four chapters.
passages.asks:
The psalm begins by remembering what God has done. Before you ask God for anything today, recount one thing he has already done for you.

Then notice who God is said to remember: the afflicted, the oppressed. Ask who in your town is crying out and not being heard, and how you might hear them.

passages.t: From the gates of death to the gates of Zion
passages.happening:
Now the man prays for himself. “Be merciful to me, O LORD; see how my enemies afflict me! Lift me up from the gates of death” (verse 13). He wants to live “that I may declare all Your praises” (verse 14).

Then he sees evil caught in its own trap. “The nations have fallen into a pit of their making; their feet are caught in the net they have hidden” (verse 15). “The wicked will return to Sheol”, it says, and it names them: “all the nations who forget God” (verse 17).

And a promise: “For the needy will not always be forgotten; nor the hope of the oppressed forever dashed” (verse 18).

The psalm ends with a call: “Rise up, O LORD, do not let man prevail” (verse 19). He asks God to “let the nations know they are but men” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
City gates were the centre of public life. Elders sat there, and legal cases were heard there. So the psalm sets two gates against each other: ‘the gates of death’ and ‘the gates of Daughter Zion’ (verse 14). The man prays to be lifted out of one doorway and set in the other, where he can praise God in public.

‘Daughter Zion’ is a loving name for Jerusalem and its people.

The pit and the net are hunters' traps. The trappers are trapped.

‘Higgaion’ and ‘Selah’ after verse 16 are words for the music. Their meaning is not certain.

Sheol is the place of the dead. ‘Return to Sheol’ means the wicked go back to the dust they came from. The psalm sets those who ‘forget God’ (verse 17) against the God who does not forget the needy (verse 18).

‘Let the nations know they are but men’ means: let the powerful remember they are mortal, frail human beings, not gods. It echoes the humble question of Psalm 8: ‘what is man?’
passages.later:
Mary's song speaks the same reversal: God “has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty” (Luke 1:53).

Jesus told of a widow who kept crying out to a judge for justice, and asked, “Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night?” (Luke 18:7).

Isaiah calls God's people to do what this psalm says God does: “Defend the fatherless and plead the case of the widow” (Isaiah 1:17).
passages.asks:
‘The needy will not always be forgotten.’ If you are the one who feels forgotten, this line is for you: not a promise that the wait will be short, but that it will not be forever.

And if you have power over others, at work or at home, verse 20 is for you: remember that you are only human.
